chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Cost-of-Carry Model, First Principles

lessons.title: Why Futures Prices Differ From Spot: Setting Up the Problem

children.text: A Number That Should Not Make Sense

Open MCX and pull up the Gold futures chain. Spot gold, converted to Indian units at the ruling exchange rate, works out to roughly ₹72,000 for 10 grams. The MCX Gold contract expiring six months out is trading at ₹74,600. Same metal, same purity, same exchange, and yet a jeweller buying today for delivery in six months pays ₹2,600 more per 10 grams than someone walking into a bullion dealer to buy gold right now. Nothing about the gold itself has changed between those two contracts. So where does that ₹2,600 come from?

body.label: Illustrative MCX Gold example
body.context: Numbers are hypothetical for this lesson, built to illustrate the mechanics. Always check MCX's live contract prices before trading.

children.text: Spot Price vs Futures Price: Two Different Promises
is what you pay today for gold delivered today, whether that is at a Zaveri Bazaar counter, a bank's gold coin scheme, or through units of a gold ETF. A

is what a buyer and a seller agree today to exchange gold for, on a fixed date months from now, at a price locked in right now. These are two different contracts for two different points in time. There is no reason to assume they should be equal, any more than a fixed deposit maturing in six months should pay the same amount as cash in your hand today.

markDefs.definition: The price for buying or selling an asset for immediate delivery, settled almost at once. For gold in India, this is usually quoted per 10 grams of 999 purity, derived from the international dollar price and the USD/INR rate.
The price agreed today for delivering (or receiving) an asset on a specified future date, fixed by an exchange-traded futures contract such as those on MCX.

children.text: If you have traded Nifty or Bank Nifty futures on the NSE, you have already seen this pattern. The current-month Nifty future almost always trades a few points above the Nifty index itself, and the gap is usually wider for the far month than the near month. MCX commodity futures behave the same way. The gap is often larger, and unlike an index future, you can point to actual physical costs, storage, insurance, financing, behind most of it.
The gap between the two prices has a name: the
. It is simply futures price minus spot price.

markDefs.definition: Futures price minus spot price for the same underlying asset. Basis is not fixed; it shrinks as a contract nears expiry and converges to zero on the expiry date itself, a mechanism covered in Chapter 2.

body.caption: F is the futures price, S is the spot price. A positive basis (futures above spot) means the market is in contango. A negative basis (futures below spot) means backwardation. Chapter 2 covers both in depth.

children.text: The basis is not unique to commodities. Every futures market has one. What changes from market to market is what mainly drives it.

body.caption: The same basis idea, across different Indian futures markets

cells: Interest cost of funding the index basket, minus expected dividend yield
Interest cost of funding the share, minus expected dividend
Interest cost plus storage and insurance; gold pays no yield to offset it
Storage capacity and how scarce a barrel is for immediate delivery right now

body.text: Every one of these futures prices is built the same way: spot price, plus whatever it costs in interest, storage and insurance to hold that asset until the contract's expiry, minus whatever income you would have earned holding it instead (a dividend for a stock, nothing at all for gold). That relationship is the cost-of-carry model, and this course exists to make you fluent in it for commodities specifically, where the physical costs are real and often large enough to trade on.

children.text: Why "The Market Expects Gold to Rise" Is the Wrong Explanation

The most common mistake a new commodity trader makes is reading the futures premium as a forecast: "futures are trading above spot, so the market must expect gold to go up." That instinct feels reasonable because it is exactly how you are taught to read an option's implied volatility or a stock's forward P/E, as a reflection of expectations. Commodity futures pricing does not work that way, and mixing up the two is where most beginner confusion about contango and backwardation starts.

columns.label: What most new traders assume
points: A higher futures price means the market expects gold to rise by expiry
A wider gap between spot and futures signals stronger bullish sentiment
Backwardation must mean the market expects prices to fall

columns.label: What the cost-of-carry model actually says
points: The gap mostly reflects financing cost, storage and insurance, not a forecast of where gold is headed
A wider gap usually means higher interest rates or higher storage and insurance cost, not stronger sentiment
Backwardation usually means the commodity is scarce for immediate delivery right now, a convenience yield story covered in Lesson 4

body.title: First read on the basis
body.question: MCX Silver's three-month futures contract trades at a wider premium to spot than MCX Gold's three-month contract does, as a percentage of price. Under the cost-of-carry model, which explanation fits best without any further information?
options: The market expects silver to rally much harder than gold over the next three months
Silver's higher day-to-day price volatility makes its futures inherently more expensive
Silver has meaningfully higher storage and insurance cost per rupee of value than gold, since it is bulkier and lower value per kilogram
MCX charges higher margins on silver contracts, which pushes up the futures price
body.explanation: Cost of carry, not sentiment, is the default explanation for a futures premium. Silver takes up far more physical storage space and needs more insurance per rupee of value than gold, since it is a bulkier, lower-value-per-kilogram metal. That physical carrying cost, not a bullish forecast, is what mainly widens silver's premium relative to gold's. Lesson 3 builds this out with the full formula.

children.text: The rest of this chapter builds the cost-of-carry formula properly. Lesson 2 shows the no-arbitrage argument that pins the futures price down, the reasoning a trader would use to lock in a riskless profit if the basis ever strayed too far from where it should be. Lesson 3 assembles the formula itself out of interest, storage and insurance. Lesson 4 adds the one piece that does not fit neatly into a formula, convenience yield, and shows why some commodities defy the simple model altogether. Chapter 2 then uses all of it to explain contango, backwardation and how the basis behaves as expiry approaches.

body.text: A futures price is not the market's forecast of where an asset is headed. It is the spot price today, adjusted for the real, measurable cost of holding that asset in your hands, or your warehouse, until the day the contract expires.

points: Spot price is for delivery now; futures price is agreed today for delivery on a fixed future date. There is no reason for the two to be equal.
Basis = Futures price − Spot price. A positive basis is contango, a negative basis is backwardation.
Every futures market has a basis, but what drives it differs: dividends and interest for stock and index futures, interest plus real storage and insurance costs for commodities like gold and silver.
The futures premium is not a forecast of the sentiment or direction of the underlying. It mostly reflects the cost of carrying the asset forward in time.
This course builds that cost-of-carry formula step by step, then applies it across gold, silver, crude oil and agri commodities on MCX.
